title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's rewriting the org as if it didn't exist
dek: Locke merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring someone now requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: A 12-year hardware company's founder lays out the concrete mechanics of an org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pits he fell into.
who: Founders driving AI org transformation, heads of HR and business leads — especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies who want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is assuming the old org and processes don't exist — ‘they logically shouldn't even exist’ — and going back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes; it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He concedes this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: HARO's lead comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Locke merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the lead must understand the business, and he picked the old partner who co-founded with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person leads, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will build Agent Builders) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people short-term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long-term one person might cover it; short-term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them in for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’ and above that ‘pilots’.

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus pool
points.body: Locke's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team with an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives a circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — with HR and functional departments holding only an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first half-year to a year of the change, the front line gets to decide.

points.h: Experience itself can become a burden
points.body: Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the most troublesome are the half-baked — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel they are very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as their foundation, but on which processes and which roles can be removed, the clear-eyed judge more easily. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill use and Agent building; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and bigger bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and that 60-point output doesn't stick around. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content drives conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-up: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Locke ran three internal rounds of sign-up: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level ten or twenty Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

points.h: To hire, you must first prove AI can't do it
points.body: After a circle picks off people from an original department, if the boss wants to backfill, logically there are only two channels: take an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Locke is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

Chen Bin says inside the company he is in fact the most radical one, often held back by everyone urging more caution. On sedimented systems like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only rework processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, SP to BP, from strategy to execution, used to take three months to half a year, now two months, doubling efficiency, but the nodes like Five Looks Three Sets are still there — it's just that what took three weeks now takes three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five, but the rotations that must happen can't be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature before choosing, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user end to the supply chain end, so it matters more there.

quotes.text: I think an AI-native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, try not to have a person do it. Think with an AI-native mindset first, and even this process should logically be restructured.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end small team with a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make functional power smaller and the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it, but the half-baked are the scary ones — their experience hasn't arrived, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill with AI, right? Prioritize AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled. And if it can't be filled, internally we say: either you find an AI management trainee to fill it, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least double the efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, now it's three meetings, two meetings.

Actually look at the real value AI brings in this industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower. And if it's lower, then you can, as it were, wait until these — people like us who are digging the pits and playing around, right? — or until Doubao, Volcano Engine and the like are doing better, and then choose. That's fine.
